speaker_role: former director of MBA admissions and financial aid at Wharton, now runs an undergraduate admissions coaching firm (Admittedly); not a former undergrad AO per the transcript, though he claims to have read tens of thousands of essays
commercial_incentive: Yes: repeatedly promotes the firm's paid essay review service and coaching.
key_insights: Decide your overall direction before drafting: know what you want to study and what evidence supports it, then choose what the essay must convey.
Essays centered on a relative or trauma usually fail by focusing on the other person; keep the focus on you and how the experience shaped you, stating the event briefly.
Do not manufacture hardship; authenticity matters and schools are starting to use technology to verify claims and enforce AI policies, with rescinded admission possible.
Admissions essays need an early hook because readers are tired and skim; write the hook last, unlike a slowly building school essay.
Avoid copying successful published essays, which worked because they were fresh; imitations become derivative.
The additional information and adversity sections are for facts you can't convey elsewhere; keep them brief and don't use them for a bonus essay.
For supplements, vary which aspects of your strategy each covers, avoid overlapping the main essay, and for 'why us' explain what you want to learn, not just contribute.
Parents should give feedback but not rewrite; adult phrasing is noticeable to experienced readers.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker says readers have 5 to 8 minutes per application.
Main essay limit stated as 650 words; additional information section about 350 words.
Speaker says UCLA received over 145,000 applications last year.
Speaker recommends choosing Common App prompt 7 (topic of your choice) and says some schools are dropping supplements.
notable_or_distinctive: Contrarian, specific guidance to write the hook last, skip mimicking successful essays, and pick the open prompt.
reliability_notes: Confident opinions from an MBA-side background with sales framing; claims about verification technology and AI detection are asserted without evidence.
